docs.title: spring-boot-guard
docs.text:
Spring Boot adapter for the guard-core-jvm engine for the JVM. The adapter is a true port of the fastapi-guard adapter behavior onto the Spring WebMVC/Boot 3.x envelope: the engine's 17-check pipeline runs per request, error responses come byte-exact from the facade response factory, and the guard.* property surface reaches every SecurityConfig field.

  • Status: 1.0.0, released (the first synchronized release)
  • Engine: com.guard-core:guard-core:4.3.3 (built from source through a composite build, see Installation)
  • Parity: the engine's every-feature matrix and the spec section table carry the family-level status

The adapter contains no security logic of its own - every decision is the engine's.

docs.title: Documentation map
docs.text:
• Installation - coordinates, engine dependency, Redis
  • API - the auto-configuration, filter, annotations, and re-exports
  • Examples - the runnable demo app

Boot 3.x is the current lane; the 4.x lane joins the test matrix next.

docs.title: Adapter parity: fastapi-guard 8.1.0 (PureASGISecurityMiddleware)
docs.text: Assessment of the W10 parity wave (2026-10-13): what fastapi-guard 8.1.0 changed, how this adapter's native idiom maps onto it, and which of the pure-streaming properties hold here. Conclusion up front: the servlet filter idiom already satisfies the cancellation and body-replay properties; the unbuffered-streaming property does NOT hold (the response wrapper buffers), which is a deliberate, documented trade of this adapter and not something this wave changes.

docs.title: What upstream shipped
docs.text:
fastapi-guard 8.1.0 (2026-10-10, #156) added PureASGISecurityMiddleware: the full screening pipeline running on raw ASGI without BaseHTTPMiddleware. It exists to win three properties the classic middleware loses to Starlette's anyio task group:

  1. No downstream wrapping that could cancel in-flight work (a client disconnect can never cancel an in-flight database call).
  2. Unbuffered response streaming (security and CORS headers injected directly on http.response.start, body bytes never held).
  3. A caching receive that replays the request body to the application after the guard reads it.

Scope note from the upstream release: decorator-driven response rules (return patterns) and custom_response_modifier need a materialized Response object; they stay on the classic middleware and both classes ship side by side.

docs.title: The idiom mapping
docs.text: This adapter's native idiom is the servlet envelope: GuardFilter, a Spring OncePerRequestFilter placed pre-routing so unmatched paths are also scanned. The servlet container hands the filter the raw request/response and the downstream chain; there is no BaseHTTPMiddleware analog to avoid - nothing ever wrapped the downstream app in a task group here. The PureASGI release validates an idiom this family already holds natively, the same way fastapi-guard's Starlette-only constraint never applied to the servlet lane.

docs.title: 1. No downstream cancelling wrap: HOLDS
docs.text: GuardFilter.doFilterInternal runs filterChain.doFilter synchronously on the same servlet thread. No coroutine scope wraps the downstream call: the guard's own suspend stages bridge through runBlocking confined to the guard entry point (the facade's xBlocking bridge convention), and even the security-bypass path's downstream leg runs under plain runBlocking, which has no cancellation source. A client disconnect cannot cancel in-flight handler work in this model; it surfaces later, as a write failure on the committed response. This is the property PureASGI exists to win on Starlette; the servlet lane never had the problem.

docs.title: 2. A caching receive that replays the body: HOLDS
docs.text: GuardHttpServletRequest (ServletGuardRequest.kt) reads the servlet input stream exactly once into a single-source byte cache and hands the downstream chain a replaying ServletInputStream: the bytes the penetration scan saw are the bytes the handler sees, with bounded prefix reads stopping the wire pull at the cap. This is the exact contract of the reference's caching receive (and Starlette's own _body cache it mirrors).

docs.title: 3. Unbuffered response streaming: DOES NOT HOLD (documented finding)
docs.text:
GuardFilter wraps the response in Spring's ContentCachingResponseWrapper and calls copyBodyToResponse() only after the facade's process_response exit path and CORS injection run. Every response body is fully materialized in memory before the first byte reaches the client: SSE streams, file downloads, and large bodies included. The wrapper is what lets the adapter post-process a handler's response before it commits (behavioral return rules, the custom response modifier, response-time metrics, CORS into the buffered response), which is the classic-middleware feature set.

This is the trade fastapi-guard 8.1.0's scope note describes, seen from the other side: response rules and the response modifier need a materialized response, so they live on the buffering idiom. The servlet adapter IS the classic middleware of the JVM family; the buffering is its cost, not a parity bug. Reported, not fixed, per the W10 scope: the fix shape, if ever needed for SSE-at-scale deployments, is a second header-pre-commit filter variant shipping beside GuardFilter (the PureASGI-beside-SecurityMiddleware pattern), not a change to GuardFilter's contract.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: Zero code changes in the 8.1.0 parity wave. Two of the three pure-streaming properties hold natively; the third (unbuffered streaming) is a documented deliberate trade of the buffering idiom this adapter is built on, priced exactly as upstream prices it: the features that need a materialized response are the features this adapter ships.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The adapter's public surface (package com.guardcore.spring). Consumers import from the adapter package, never from the engine coordinates directly.

docs.title: Auto-configuration
docs.text:
GuardSecurityAutoConfiguration wires the whole integration:

  • a SecurityConfig bean built from the guard.* properties
  • the facade GuardMiddleware (engine-facing GuardMiddlewareProtocol)
  • the GuardFilter servlet filter that runs the 17-check pipeline per request (OncePerRequestFilter, pre-routing so unmatched paths are enveloped)
  • the optional Redis option and the eager-init lifecycle

docs.title: GuardFilter
docs.text: SecurityFilter behavior (the SecurityMiddleware.dispatch port): preflight handling, exclude-path scoping, security bypass, pipeline block before the handler, behavioral usage rules, and processResponse (behavioral return rules + metrics + security headers + CORS) after it. The servlet protocol impls (ServletGuardRequest, ServletGuardResponse, ServletGuardResponseFactory) mirror the reference's Starlette shapes byte-exact, including the bounded read_body_prefix.

docs.title: Decorator annotations
docs.text:
The facade SecurityDecorator factories 1:1 (same parameter surface, same defaults) applied per handler method with method-identity route ids:

@GuardRequireIp, @GuardBlockCountries, @GuardAllowCountries, @GuardBlockClouds, @GuardBypass, @GuardRateLimit, @GuardGeoRateLimit, @GuardUsageMonitor, @GuardReturnMonitor, @GuardBehaviorAnalysis, @GuardSuspiciousFrequency, @GuardRequireHttps, @GuardRequireAuth, @GuardApiKeyAuth, @GuardRequireAuthorizationHeader, @GuardRequireHeaders, @GuardBlockUserAgents, @GuardContentTypeFilter, @GuardMaxRequestSize, @GuardRequireReferrer, @GuardCustomValidation, @GuardDetectionExclusion, @GuardTimeWindow, @GuardSuspiciousDetection, @GuardHoneypotDetection.

Callable factory parameters (verifiers, validators) reference Spring beans by name (verifierBean / validatorBean; bean types RouteAuthVerifier and CustomRouteValidator).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: guard.* properties bind 122 of the 129 SecurityConfig fields (relaxed binding maps guard.redis-url to redisUrl); the 7 object-typed fields (geo_ip_handler, cloud_ip_store, custom_request_check, auth_verifier, custom_response_modifier, on_error, on_block) wire through SecurityConfigCustomizer beans, so all 129 are reachable. Field-by-field semantics live in the engine's configuration reference.

docs.title: Re-exports
docs.text: ReExports.kt re-exports the engine's user-facing types (the fastapi-guard guard/__init__.py convention): SecurityConfig, SecurityConfigBuilder, SecurityDecorator, RouteConfig, the handler managers (RedisManager, RateLimitManager, IpBanManager, IpInfoManager, CloudManager, SecurityHeadersManager, BehaviorTracker), and the protocol types.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Initialization is lazy on the first request behind a lock, with a 503 Service temporarily unavailable + Retry-After: 5 response when Redis is unavailable and guard.redis-fail-open is false. Set guard.eager-init=true to initialize at context startup.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
examples/demo-boot is a runnable Boot application with guarded and open routes, live Redis-backed rate limiting, and per-route decorator configs.

git clone https://github.com/Guard-Core/spring-boot-guard.git
cd spring-boot-guard
git clone https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core-jvm.git guard-core-jvm
git -C guard-core-jvm checkout 09dfddf
docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine
./gradlew :examples:demo-boot:bootRun

Quick start in your own app (the whole integration):

@SpringBootApplication
class App

@RestController
class Routes {
    @GuardBypass(checks = ["all"])
    @GetMapping("/health")
    fun health() = mapOf("status" to "ok")

    @GuardRateLimit(requests = 5, window = 60)
    @GetMapping("/api/tight")
    fun tight() = mapOf("ok" to true)
}

guard:
  enable-redis: true
  redis-url: redis://localhost:6379
  blocked-user-agents:
    - "BadBot"
  endpoint-rate-limits:
    "[/api/limited]":
      requests: 5
      window: 60

GuardSecurityAutoConfiguration wires the SecurityConfig bean, the facade GuardMiddleware, and the GuardFilter that runs the 17-check pipeline per request. See API for the annotation set and the property surface.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 17 or newer (Spring Boot 3.x baseline)
  • Spring Boot 3.x (built and tested against 3.5.16; the 4.x lane joins next)
  • Redis 6+ for the distributed features (rate limiting, IP bans, behavioral state) - guard.redis-url, default redis://localhost:6379

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
Published on Maven Central:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.guard-core:spring-boot-guard:1.0.0")
}

The group ID is com.guard-core (the Central Portal namespace); Kotlin packages stay com.guardcore.*.

docs.title: Engine dependency (includeBuild + dependency substitution)
docs.text:
Consumers resolve the engine artifact com.guard-core:guard-core from Maven Central. This repository's own build pins the engine from source instead: CI and local builds check out Guard-Core/guard-core-jvm at the pinned ref 09dfddf as the sibling directory ./guard-core-jvm, and settings.gradle.kts substitutes the declared coordinates com.guard-core:guard-core:4.3.3 / com.guard-core:guard-core-engine:4.3.3 with the included build's projects. The declared dependency coordinates stay com.guard-core:guard-core:4.3.3 (lockstep version per the family versioning law).

git clone https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core-jvm.git guard-core-jvm
git -C guard-core-jvm checkout 09dfddf
./gradlew build

The engine directory resolves in order: -PguardCoreJvmDir=<path>, GUARD_CORE_JVM_DIR, ./guard-core-jvm, ../guard-core-jvm.

Set GUARD_CORE_USE_COMPOSITE=false to build without the composite: the declared coordinates then resolve from the repositories (mavenLocal first, then Maven Central) - this is how the release workflow proves the published artifact graph.

docs.title: Dependency locking
docs.text: gradle.lockfile is committed and enforced on every resolution: a dependency change without ./gradlew --write-locks fails the build. CI additionally scans the lockfile with osv-scanner (fail on any known vulnerability).

docs.title: Release runbook (spring-boot-guard)
docs.text: Adapter release choreography. The shared mechanics (Portal namespace, user token, GPG, publishing limits, rollback semantics) are documented once in the engine repo: guard-core-jvm docs/release.md. This file covers what differs here.

docs.title: Versioning law
docs.text:
• Artifact com.guard-core:spring-boot-guard; version 1.0.0 (fresh family version). The version lives in build.gradle.kts; the tag must equal it.
  • The engine lockstep pin lives in gradle/libs.versions.toml (guardCore = "4.3.3"); it moves only when the engine train moves.
  • Tags are bare vX.Y.z only (v1.0.0). The tag-consistency job audits this (the guard-core-rs invisible-rule incident on refs/tags/v4.3.2 is the standing lesson).
  • groupId com.guard-core; Kotlin packages stay com.guardcore.*.

docs.title: Version-flip checklist (the release PR)
docs.text:
The workflow enforces this: tagging without the flip fails tag-consistency with an explicit message.

  • [ ] build.gradle.kts: version = "1.0.0-SNAPSHOT" -> version = "1.0.0".
  • [ ] gradle/libs.versions.toml: guardCore still reads the lockstep engine version (4.3.3).
  • [ ] The GUARD_CORE_JVM_REF pin (ci.yml + settings comments) already points at the released engine SHA (bumped at train time, per the family spec).
  • [ ] CHANGELOG.md: ## [Unreleased] renamed to ## [1.0.0] - YYYY-MM-DD with the engine pin stated.
  • [ ] CI green on the release PR; merge it; tag the merge commit.

docs.title: Release choreography
docs.text:
Hard order: the engine artifacts MUST be live on Maven Central first. The pre-flight job checks both com.guard-core:guard-core-engine and com.guard-core:guard-core at the pinned lockstep version on repo1.maven.org and refuses to run anything if they are not (engine-before-adapters, enforced mechanically, not on the honor system).

  1. Complete the engine train first: guard-core-jvm tagged, released, Portal deployments released, repo1 answering 200 for both engine artifacts (engine docs/release.md, steps 1 and 5).
  2. Merge the version-flip PR.
  3. Tag: git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0. Gates run in order: pre-flight (engine live) -> tests at tag (composite ON, same as ci.yml) -> tag-consistency (bare tag equals the in-file version).
  4. Create the GitHub release for v1.0.0. The publish job:
  5. verifies the four secrets are set (Portal user token + GPG key);
  6. checks repo1 for this exact artifact and skips if already live (changed-only rerun safety);
  7. builds the staging bundle with GUARD_CORE_USE_COMPOSITE=false, so the engine dependency resolves from the repositories (mavenLocal, then Maven Central) - the published artifact graph, not the composite checkout;
  8. uploads the bundle to the Central Portal Publisher API (publishingType=USER_MANAGED) and polls until VALIDATED.
  9. Release the deployment in the Portal UI (central.sonatype.com, Publishing -> Deployments).
  10. Verify liveness: curl -f https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/guard-core/spring-boot-guard/1.0.0/spring-boot-guard-1.0.0.pom

docs.title: Post-release audits (per train)
docs.text:
1. Release page for v1.0.0 exists with the expected notes (per-tag audit; the php v4.3.1 lesson).
  2. repo1 answers 200 for the artifact (the same check the workflow uses).
  3. No deployment left VALIDATED/PENDING in the Portal.
  4. The GUARD_CORE_JVM_REF pin (ci.yml checkout + settings comments) moves to the released engine SHA AT TRAIN TIME, before the consumer tags: the adapter's at-tag tests must run against the engine that actually ships (the family spec pins this; a pin bump is an ordinary development PR).

docs.title: Rerun safety, failure recovery, rollback
docs.text: Same rules as the engine runbook: workflow_dispatch re-drives skip anything already live on repo1; a VALIDATED deployment you do not want gets Dropped in the Portal; published artifacts are immutable - no rollback after the Portal Release click, only a fix version.
